question: Which scalar statistic extracted from a data-versus-reference classifier gives the broadest multivariate goodness-of-fit sensitivity to unknown collider anomalies?

key_findings.claim: The study treats model-independent collider search as a goodness-of-fit problem rather than as a test against one fixed beyond-Standard-Model alternative.
key_findings.evidence: A flexible neural-network or kernel classifier is retrained to distinguish each observed sample from a much larger simulated Standard Model reference. Its output both compresses the multivariate event and defines likelihood-ratio, optimized count, accuracy, AUC, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics.

key_findings.claim: Across the selected toy and dimuon alternatives, the classifier-derived extended likelihood ratio is the most consistently sensitive statistic, while no goodness-of-fit test is uniformly optimal against all alternatives.
key_findings.evidence: The one-dimensional suite contains two localized excesses, a smooth tail distortion with and without a rate change, and a tail depletion. The dimuon suite contains two resonances and a non-resonant contact interaction under two mass cuts. The LRT is competitive throughout and is the only displayed test sensitive to the toy depletion H4, whereas conventional chi-square power varies strongly with binning and KS favors some broad shape effects.

key_findings.claim: The proposed optimized tail-count statistic gains slightly on resonant excesses but can fail sharply on non-resonant or depletion alternatives.
key_findings.evidence: The Pois statistic scans a classifier threshold and compares the observed and expected counts above it. Its one-sided right-tail construction performs comparably to or better than LRT for peaks, yet the paper reports poor sensitivity for non-resonant effects and especially for a missing-event region. This is a built-in directional bias rather than a generic anomaly score.

key_findings.claim: Empirical calibration includes classifier fitting and threshold optimization, but only about 400 null experiments are used, far too few to validate collider discovery tails directly.
key_findings.evidence: Every data sample is used in-sample to retrain the classifier and compute the statistic; its null law is then estimated by rerunning the complete workflow about 400 times, with about 100 alternative repetitions. This can calibrate the shown power range if simulation is exact, but a 400-sample empirical null cannot resolve five-sigma p-values or thoroughly diagnose tail miscalibration.

key_findings.claim: The central comparison assumes an accurately reproducible Standard Model reference and omits the nuisance uncertainty that dominates real collider goodness-of-fit deployment.
key_findings.evidence: The method assumes a simulated reference much larger than data and treats expected binned counts as error-free in the toy chi-square test. In the dimuon study the authors explicitly neglect systematic uncertainty and point to a separate strategy. Thus the reported power curves test anomaly morphology under an idealized null, not coverage under detector, theory, calibration, or finite-Monte-Carlo misspecification.

key_findings.claim: Kernel logistic regression offers a large practical speed advantage in the reported setup, but runtime and statistical power are not compared under one controlled compute budget.
key_findings.evidence: The neural classifier is trained for 300,000 epochs in the one-dimensional case and takes order-hours per fit on a CPU cluster, while the Nyström kernel model takes order-seconds on an RTX 6000. Architectures, regularization, hardware, and fitting schemes differ, and the figures emphasize test power rather than a power-versus-compute frontier.

method.core_idea: Fit a flexible classifier between observed collider events and a high-statistics Standard Model reference, then compare several one-dimensional goodness-of-fit statistics computed from that learned density-ratio proxy.
method.mechanism: For every pseudo-experiment, retrain either a small neural network or Nyström kernel logistic regressor; evaluate an extended log-likelihood ratio, a scanned right-tail Poisson count, optimized accuracy, rate-aware AUC, output-space KS, and rate-only significance; estimate each null distribution by complete-workflow repetitions; and compare power curves across structured signal injections.
assumptions: The simulated reference accurately represents the full Standard Model event distribution and expected rate.
A much larger reference sample makes its Monte Carlo error negligible.
Repeating the same adaptive fit under the null adequately calibrates in-sample classifier statistics.
The chosen neural and kernel hyperparameters control flexible-alternative overfitting across signal morphologies.
The selected one-dimensional and five-dimensional alternatives cover enough anomaly types to support a broad-sensitivity comparison.
Neglected detector and theory systematics can later be incorporated without reversing the ranking.
Hundreds of pseudo-experiments suffice for the confidence levels displayed.

techniques.role: Learns a data-to-reference density-ratio proxy through binary classification.
Aggregates learned event scores and rate information into an extended likelihood-ratio statistic.
Scans a classifier threshold for the most significant right-tail event-count discrepancy.
Uses Gaussian-kernel logistic regression with Nyström centers as a fast nonparametric alternative fit.
Calibrates adaptive statistics by rerunning training on reference-distributed pseudo-data.
Compares the fraction of detected injected signals across null confidence thresholds.

evaluations.setting: A one-dimensional unit-mean exponential null with 2,000 expected events and four qualitatively different injected departures.
evaluations.metric: Power as a function of null score threshold over roughly 400 null and 100 alternative pseudo-experiments.
evaluations.result: LRT and the optimized Poisson tail test lead on average; LRT alone remains sensitive to the tail-depletion benchmark, and chi-square performance changes with binning.
evaluations.baseline: Input-space KS and chi-square tests, rate-only significance, output-space KS, optimized accuracy, and rate-aware AUC.

evaluations.setting: Five-dimensional simulated LHC dimuon events with 60 or 100 GeV invariant-mass cuts and two Z-prime resonances or a dimension-six contact interaction.
evaluations.metric: Power curves for neural and kernel classifier-derived statistics.
evaluations.result: LRT and Pois dominate the displayed classifier metrics, but Pois loses its advantage for the non-resonant benchmark.
evaluations.baseline: Accuracy, extended AUC, output KS, and normalization-only significance using the same learned classifier.

evaluations.setting: Per-pseudo-experiment neural versus kernel alternative fitting.
evaluations.metric: Reported order of runtime and qualitative power.
evaluations.result: Kernel fits take order-seconds on one GPU versus order-hours for neural fits on a CPU cluster in the authors' configurations; no matched-budget frontier is given.
evaluations.baseline: A small sigmoid MLP and a Gaussian Nyström kernel logistic model.

limitations: Author-stated: no goodness-of-fit test is optimal against every possible discrepancy.
Author-stated: the optimized Poisson-tail statistic can fail strongly on non-resonant and depletion signals.
Author-stated: dimuon systematic uncertainties are neglected in this workshop study.
Author-stated: more work is required to maximize the LRT algorithms' potential.
Reviewer inference: only about 400 null repetitions cannot validate extreme discovery-level tails.
Reviewer inference: the reference distribution and expected rate are treated as essentially known, so misspecified simulation can be learned as a false anomaly.
Reviewer inference: statistics are fit and evaluated in-sample; calibration is valid only insofar as every source of adaptation is faithfully repeated under the null.
Reviewer inference: the signal panel is small, hand-designed, and low-dimensional relative to full collider records.
Reviewer inference: neural and kernel runtime comparisons use different hardware and tuning protocols.
Reviewer inference: this seven-page workshop paper delegates important model-selection, nuisance, and reproduction details to earlier papers rather than testing them here.
failure_modes: A detector drift or Monte Carlo modeling error produces a highly significant classifier discrepancy that is mistaken for new physics.
Scanning a tail threshold on the same sample inflates significance when the null calibration omits any part of the scan or tuning process.
A deficit or diffuse interaction has no concentrated high-score excess and is nearly invisible to the one-sided Pois statistic.
The learned alternative overfits statistical fluctuations, shifting the null tail beyond what a small calibration ensemble resolves.
A rare narrow anomaly is diluted by global accuracy or AUC despite being scientifically important.
A fixed model capacity is too rigid for one signal morphology and too flexible for another, changing power in an unreported way.
Retraining hundreds of neural classifiers per analysis becomes computationally prohibitive when event dimension and sample size grow.
reusable_insights: Evaluate anomaly detectors as full statistical tests: calibration, type-I error, power, and nuisance robustness matter more than classifier AUC alone.
A learned likelihood ratio can aggregate excesses, deficits, rate, and shape more broadly than a one-sided cut-and-count statistic.
Any adaptive threshold, representation, or hyperparameter selection must be included inside every null-calibration repetition.
Benchmark panels should vary locality, sign, rate, smoothness, and feature interactions rather than testing only resonant excesses.
Separate power from compute by comparing methods on matched wall-clock or simulation budgets.
Discovery-tail validation needs analytical asymptotics, importance sampling, or other rare-event calibration beyond a few hundred null trials.
Nuisance-aware tests should expose which learned discrepancy persists after profiling detector and theory uncertainty.
open_questions: Can the NPLM statistic retain calibrated coverage when detector, theory, luminosity, and finite-reference uncertainties are jointly profiled?
How can five-sigma null tails be validated without millions of complete classifier retrainings?
Would cross-fitting or conditional randomization improve robustness relative to in-sample evaluation without sacrificing too much power?
Which diverse, adversarial anomaly suite best measures model-independent power rather than benchmark-specific tuning?
Can batchwise or streaming density-ratio summaries match a full-data test under bounded compute and storage?
How should a significant learned discrepancy be localized and translated into a falsifiable physics follow-up while controlling multiplicity?
When does a learned deep kernel dominate a classifier likelihood ratio under an equal compute and calibration budget?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning New Physics from a Machine
competitive_landscape.difference: D'Agnolo and Wulzer introduce the neural flexible-alternative likelihood-ratio method, return a calibrated p-value, and localize discrepant phase space. The workshop paper does not introduce that core NPLM construction; it compares multiple scalar tests on neural and kernel instantiations and adds the optimized Poisson-tail statistic.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Multivariate New Physics
competitive_landscape.difference: The earlier NPLM study develops the neural implementation and the same dimuon application in much greater depth. This workshop comparison reuses that line of work to ask whether likelihood ratio, count, AUC, accuracy, or KS is the better learned goodness-of-fit summary.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Deep Kernels for Non-Parametric Two-Sample Tests
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu and colleagues train deep kernels to maximize test power, provide consistency for the adaptive test, and compare with classifier two-sample testing. The workshop paper instead emphasizes extended event rates and likelihood-ratio fitting for collider searches, with empirical rather than general statistical guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Minimax optimal testing by classification
competitive_landscape.difference: Gerber, Han, and Polyanskiy prove near-minimax sample complexity for classification-accuracy testing in several goodness-of-fit and likelihood-free settings. Their results sharpen when a simple classifier statistic is theoretically sufficient, whereas this workshop finds empirical accuracy inferior to its fitted likelihood ratio on the selected collider alternatives.

competitive_landscape.title: Goodness of fit by Neyman-Pearson testing
competitive_landscape.difference: The same core team later gives a fuller comparison of NPLM with classifier-based strategies and argues that it is especially sensitive to small, diverse departures. That paper is the primary follow-up for the workshop's broad-sensitivity claim and should supersede the short workshop treatment for methodology details.

competitive_landscape.title: Anomaly-aware summary statistic from data batches
competitive_landscape.difference: Grosso parallelizes NPLM over batches and aggregates local density ratios for large or streaming samples, directly attacking the repeated-fit compute and storage bottleneck left visible here. It reports recovery or improvement over a full-data test, but nuisance and extreme-tail validation remain separate questions.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A learned extended likelihood-ratio statistic has broader model-independent sensitivity than common classifier metrics, while a new optimized count statistic can improve resonant-signal power at the cost of severe non-resonant failures.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper retrains neural and kernel classifiers over repeated pseudo-experiments and compares six learned summaries, plus classical one-dimensional tests, on four toy departures and three dimuon signals under two selections.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful contribution is the controlled warning that the statistic placed on top of an anomaly classifier determines which anomalies remain visible; AUC or accuracy is not automatically a good scientific test. The NPLM likelihood-ratio machinery and dimuon setup substantially predate this workshop paper, and the later 2023 full treatment is stronger evidence. The proposed tail count is interpretable but intentionally one-sided, while idealized simulation and shallow null tails leave real discovery calibration unresolved.

reviewer_notes: Read and visually checked all seven pages, including both multi-panel power figures, formulas, references, and checklist. Competitors were checked at primary arXiv and PMLR records on 2026-08-23. Source lineage is a direct workshop-PDF route: the stable URL hash identifies the ML4PS 2022 file itself, not an arXiv or archival-proceedings record.
